newsitem.title: BELGIUM: U.S., Chinese defence chiefs discuss better ties.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Chinese defence chiefs discuss better ties.

text.p: In an unusual television call between Belgium and Hawaii, U.S. and Chinese defence ministers on Tuesday stressed the importance of improving Washington- Beijing ties despite differences over Taiwan and other issues.

The 30-minute "teleconference" between U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, in Belgium for a NATO meeting, and Chinese Defence Minister Chi Haotian, winding up a two-week visit to the United States in Hawaii, was "very cordial", according to Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon.

Bacon said both men stressed the importance of improving bilateral relations, which now appear to be back on track after plunging in disputes over arms proliferation, human rights, trade and Taiwan, which Beijing considers a renegade province of China.

"We still have differences, but we can manage those. This was a very good visit for both countries," Perry told Chi in the private television link. The Chinese defence chief sat at a table in Hawaii next to U.S. Navy Admiral Joseph Prueher, commander of U.S. forces in the Pacific.

Chi, who held talks with with Perry and President Bill Clinton in Washington last week before moving on to visit U.S. Pacific military headquarters and other bases, thanked Perry for giving his personal attention to the visit.
He said "China and the United States share common interests and responsibilities" and that he looked forward to further cooperation in 1997.
"The question of Taiwan should and can be resolved," Chi told Perry.

The United States, under the 1972 Shanghai Communique, recognises Beijing as the sole government of China, but maintains unofficial relations with Taiwan and continues to sell arms to the island located off China.

Despite differences on Taiwan, trade and Chinese arms sales to Pakistan and Iran, the United States and China are moving to improve relations based on areas of mutual interest such as a desire for peace in Korea and economic stability in the western Pacific.

Chi announced last week that China has tentatively agreed to allow continued U.S. warship visits to Hong Kong after the British colony is returned toi China in mid-1999. They also agreed to high-level exchange visits by military officers next year and exchange visits by U.S. and Chinese warships.
But in a blunt speech to U.S. military officers in Washington last week, Chi said that China refuses to renounce the use of force to reclaim Taiwan, which Beijing considers a rogue province.

"We hope to see a peaceful settlement, yet we refuse to renounce the use of force," the visiting minister told officers at the military's National Defence University. He said the Beijing governmment would "not sit idly by" and allow Taiwan leaders continue "conniving" to split China.
Chi's policy statement was not new, but his comments on a visit to improve U.S.-China relations emphasised the importance that Communist China gives to reclaiming democratic Taiwan.

Chi urged Washington, which earlier this year dispatched two aircraft carriers to the region and accused China of trying to influence Taiwan's presidential elections with a show of military force in the Taiwan Strait, to let Beijing and Taipei settle their differences without interference.
